items.context:
You ramp a feed valve up and back down without waiting, log it, and plot flow
against valve position. The points fall on a loop rather than a line.

What is the loop telling you?
items.why:
The same valve position shows up twice with two different flows, once while the
valve is opening and once while it is closing. On this loop a valve at 57.6 %
sits at 8.578 going up and 8.997 coming down, and would settle at 8.790 if left
alone. Nothing is broken. The loop is dynamic, so it is still catching up with
an input that keeps moving.
items.true: The flow depends on where the flow just was
false: One of the two sensors is out of calibration
The valve and the flow are simply unrelated
The record covers too short a period

items.context:
You plot the same two columns from a year of plant archive, taken while the loop
was in automatic. Instead of a loop you get a diffuse cloud.

What does that tell you about the record?
items.why:
Under automatic control the valve rattles around the operating point every
sample instead of ramping, so no branch of a loop ever gets traced out. Measured
on one run of the archive, the valve's standard deviation is 1.98 % and its
correlation with the flow is +0.69: a trend, and no hysteresis. This is the same
fact as the closed-loop identification problem at the end of the session, and it
is why the session simulates the open-loop record rather than looking for one in
the archive.
items.true: The controller never let the valve ramp, so the record cannot show the loop
false: The archive is sampled too slowly to resolve anything
The flow meter and the valve are on different time bases
The loop is at steady state, so there is nothing to see

items.context: A feature column is **leaking**. What does that mean?
items.why:
Ask it of every column: would this value have been available at the moment the
prediction was due? That one question catches the direction of the shift, a lab
assay logged against sampling time rather than result time, and a `faultNumber`
column that somebody wrote down after the run. In control the same property has
a different name: a feature that uses only the present and the past is causal.
items.true: It carries information you would not have had when the prediction was due
false: It has been scaled differently from the other columns
It has more missing values than the rows around it
It came from an instrument that was out of calibration

items.context:
`shift(1)` leaves a null in the first row of each record, because that row has no
previous value.

What should you do with those rows?
items.why:
Their past lies outside the run, so there is nothing to recover. Filling with zero
invents a loop at zero flow and asks the fit to explain a step that never
happened. Losing one row per run costs nothing.
false: Fill them with zero
Fill them with the column mean
Carry the next value backwards

items.context:
A fit on three-minute samples returns `a = 0.7529` and `b = 0.0322`.

What do those two numbers become?
items.why:
`tau = -dt / ln(a)` and `K = b / (1 - a)`. The output is minutes and flow per
percent of valve, which a plant engineer who knows that feed line can check
against what they know about it. An accuracy score cannot be checked that way,
which is the reason this session converts the coefficients at all.
items.true: A time constant of 10.6 min and a gain of 0.1304
false: An accuracy of 75% and a prediction error of 0.03
A 10.6 minute delay before the valve acts on the flow
Nothing at all until you have a held-out test set

items.context:
Several archive channels come back with `a` near 0.99, which converts to a time
constant of about 298 minutes on a three-minute sampler.

What should you conclude?
items.why:
Consecutive rows are near-copies, `a` lands in the steep part of the conversion,
and the fitted time constant mostly reflects the sampling rate and the noise.
Treat a fitted `a` above about 0.99 as a warning rather than a result. Reported
as a score instead, those channels would have looked excellent, because
predicting that a slow channel does not change is easy.
items.true: The samples sit too close together for those loops
false: Those loops genuinely take several hours to settle down
The fit needs more lag columns to converge
Those channels should be dropped as broken

items.context:
Fitted on a year of ordinary plant history, a model says more cooling water goes
with a hotter reactor.

Is the model wrong, the data wrong, or the question wrong?
items.why:
The temperature controller opened the cooling water valve because the reactor got
hot, so in the record every increase in cooling follows an increase in
temperature. You wanted to know what happens when *you* open the valve, which is
the opposite causal direction, and a tightly controlled record holds almost no
evidence about it. Do not repair the sign by deleting terms. Move the setpoint,
or add a small deliberate excitation.
items.true: The question; the controller caused that correlation
false: The model; it needs a longer record to settle
The data; the cooling water sensor reads backwards
The model; the sign should be flipped by hand

items.context:
A step test sets the valve, waits for the flow to settle, and records the pair.
Why does that need no column holding the past?
items.why:
Whatever the loop was doing before, once it settles the only thing left is the
relationship between input and output, so the past carries no extra information.
Normal operation cannot afford to wait, so the history is still in there, and a
table that omits it is asking a question the data cannot answer. Note the third
distractor: the loop is dynamic either way, it has simply finished responding.
items.true: Waiting for steady state erases the history on purpose
false: Step tests use more precise instruments than a historian
A step test records fewer points
At steady state the loop has no dynamics to begin with

items.context:
The plant archive holds 20 fault types, each simulated 20 times, so one
experiment is the pair `(faultNumber, simulationRun)`. A classmate writes:

```python
pl.col("xmeas_4").shift(1).over("simulationRun")
```

They check the column, see nulls in it, and move on. What is wrong?
items.why:
Run 1 of fault 1 and run 1 of fault 4 are different plants that share a run
number, so grouping by `simulationRun` alone merges them. Count the nulls: a
correct shift leaves exactly one per experiment, so 400 of them. `shift(1)`
alone leaves 1 and fixes no boundaries, `.over("simulationRun")` leaves 20 and
fixes 19 of 399, and only `.over("faultNumber", "simulationRun")` fixes all of
them. Half a group key is more dangerous than none, because the nulls make it
look like it worked.
items.true: It groups by half the key, so most boundaries are still wrong
false: Nothing, since `simulationRun` already separates the experiments
`.over()` reverses the direction of the shift
`shift(1)` cannot be combined with `.over()` in Polars

items.context:
A dropout leaves a hole in a dataset holding a valve position `u` and the flow
`y` that valve sets. You put the rows back on a fixed grid, and now some rows are
null in both columns.

Which fill is defensible?
items.why:
A control system genuinely holds its last commanded valve position until it
writes a new one, so the carried value is what physically happened. Nothing held
the flow steady: an invented `y` becomes a row you then fit against, and least
squares cannot tell a measurement from a guess. Keep a mask column either way,
because a table that cannot say which of its numbers were measured is a table
nobody can audit.
false: Forward-fill both, since a gap is a gap
Forward-fill `y` and leave `u` null
Fill both with the column mean so nothing is missing
